rulesetReview.currentText: Five players per team on court. Substitutions can be made at stoppages when the officials allow.
rulesetReview.section: Arts. 4 and 19 (2024 numbering; may shift in 2026)
rulesetReview.note: Believed correct; OBR 2026 PDF could not be opened.

rulesetReview.currentText: Four quarters of 10 minutes. Overtime periods are 5 minutes.
rulesetReview.note: Believed correct (FIBA 4x10, OT 5 min); not verified in an opened source.

rulesetReview.currentText: Field goals count 2 points, or 3 points from beyond the three-point line (6.75 m from the basket). Each successful free throw counts 1 point.
rulesetReview.correctedText: Field goals count 2 points, or 3 points from behind the three-point line. The line is 6.75 m from the point under the centre of the basket, except near the corners where the straight sections are 6.60 m away. Each successful free throw counts 1 point.
rulesetReview.note: Correction adds the 6.60 m corner distance (secondary source snippet; some sites reverse the two figures). Confirm against the FIBA Equipment document.

rulesetReview.currentText: The offence has 24 seconds to attempt a shot that hits the rim. In some situations, such as an offensive rebound, the clock resets to 14 seconds.
rulesetReview.correctedText: The team in control has 24 seconds to shoot: the ball must leave the shooter's hand before the signal and then touch the ring or go in. If a shot touches the ring and the same team regains control, the clock resets to 14 seconds; if the opponents gain control it resets to 24.
rulesetReview.note: Original wording ('attempt a shot that hits the rim') blurred the release requirement. Other 14-second resets (e.g. some fouls/violations in the frontcourt) exist but were not verified.

rulesetReview.currentText: A team must move the ball from its backcourt into its frontcourt within 8 seconds.
An offensive player may not stay in the opponents' restricted area for more than 3 consecutive seconds while their team controls the ball in the frontcourt.
rulesetReview.note: Believed correct (game clock running is also a condition); not verified. FIBA has no defensive 3-second rule — that is NBA-only.

rulesetReview.currentText: Travelling (moving the pivot foot illegally), double dribble, carrying the ball and returning it to the backcourt give possession to the opponents.
rulesetReview.note: Broadly correct as a summary; 'carrying' is treated under illegal dribble rather than as a separately named violation. Not verified.

rulesetReview.currentText: A player is disqualified after 5 fouls. From the fifth team foul in a quarter, fouls (other than offensive fouls) lead to two free throws.
rulesetReview.section: Arts. 41 (foul limits) and 42 (team fouls) in the 2026 edition
rulesetReview.note: Team-foul part matches secondary sources (s8). But the 2026 edition (in force 1 Oct 2026) changed foul categories: flagrant fouls and Category-1 technicals count towards game disqualification, disruptive fouls and Category-2 technicals do not (s2/s3 snippets). How these interact with the 5-foul limit could not be verified — review once the OBR 2026 text is opened. Article numbers moved by one in 2026 (s1).

rulesetReview.currentText: Touching a shot on its downward flight above the rim, or touching the ball while it is in the basket area, is not allowed.
rulesetReview.note: Simplified: FIBA goaltending requires the ball to be entirely above ring level on its downward flight; basket interference covers touching the ball/ring/backboard in various situations. 2026: Instant Replay may review goaltending/interference after a foul at any time in the game (s3).

rulesetReview.currentText: Four quarters of 12 minutes; overtime periods are 5 minutes.
rulesetReview.note: Widely known to be correct, but the NBA rulebook could not be opened and snippets did not show the text.

rulesetReview.currentText: 23 ft 9 in (7.24 m) from the basket at the top, 22 ft (6.71 m) in the corners.
rulesetReview.note: Consistent with secondary sources (s7); official NBA Rule 1 text not opened.

rulesetReview.currentText: A player is disqualified after 6 personal fouls.
A defender may not stay in the lane for more than 3 seconds unless actively guarding an opponent.
rulesetReview.note: Believed correct; penalty is a technical foul (one free throw). Only low-quality secondary pages were found.

newRulePoints.text: A new edition of the FIBA Official Basketball Rules (2026) came into force worldwide on 1 October 2026, replacing the 2024 rules; some national bodies may phase it in later. Article numbers shifted, e.g. foul limits are now Art. 41 and team fouls Art. 42.

From 2026 the unsportsmanlike foul is replaced by two types: a disruptive foul (e.g. a tactical foul stopping a fast break without a legitimate play on the ball) that does not count towards game disqualification, and a flagrant foul (reckless, dangerous or excessive contact) that does.
newRulePoints.section: Rule changes 2026 summary (Arts. 37-38 per secondary sources)

newRulePoints.text: From 2026 technical fouls are split into two categories. Category 1 (e.g. disrespect to officials, taunting, offensive language/gestures, simulation) counts towards game disqualification; Category 2 does not.
Reported (NBL summary, not yet verified in the OBR text): a player is disqualified after two Category-1 technicals, two flagrant fouls, or one of each.

From 2026 the Instant Replay System may review a goaltending or basket-interference violation after a foul at any time, and whether the thrower-in still held the ball when a defensive foul occurred in the last 2 minutes of the 4th quarter or overtime.
The 2026 rules clarify (Art. 15) what counts as continuous movement and when a player is in the act of shooting, which affects whether a foul gives free throws.
FIBA mini-basketball (U12) uses a 2.60 m basket and size 5 ball; national federations may use lower baskets and smaller balls for younger groups.

From 2025-26, an unsuccessful shot from at least 36 ft in the last 3 seconds of quarters 1–3, on a play starting in the backcourt, counts as a team shot attempt, not a player's — a statistics rule, not a scoring change.
From 2025-26, when a coach challenges an out-of-bounds call, the Replay Center official (not the on-court crew chief) decides whether a proximate foul should have been called.

claims.statement: A Cochrane review found good evidence that semi-rigid or air-cast ankle braces reduce ankle sprains in high-risk sports including basketball, while a protective effect of high-top shoes was not established.

claims.topic: Balance and neuromuscular training for ankles
claims.statement: Systematic reviews support balance/neuromuscular exercise programmes and ankle braces as the most effective measures against ankle sprains in basketball. Trials are few and varied, so exact effect sizes are uncertain.
claims.section: Bellows & Wong 2018; J Clin Med 2024 review

claims.statement: Meta-analyses of neuromuscular training report the largest ACL-risk reductions in athletes under 18. Programmes emphasising plyometrics and strengthening did better than balance-only work.
In meta-regression, more completed sessions, more exercise variety and coach verbal feedback on technique were linked to better injury reduction. Compliance matters as much as programme choice.

Knee collapsing inward (abduction), stiff landings with little knee bend and asymmetric landings are linked to later ACL injury in young female athletes. Coach soft, knees-over-toes, two-footed landings, though lab gains do not always translate into fewer injuries.
Most strong evidence for ACL-prevention programmes comes from soccer and handball players over 14; basketball-specific trials are fewer, so results are partly extrapolated.
A large simulation study recommended a launch angle around 52° with slight backspin, aiming slightly towards the back of the rim. Many players release flatter than this.
Modelling work argues the optimal release conditions differ by player (height, release speed and consistency), so a single 'perfect angle' should not be forced on everyone.
FIBA mini-basketball scales equipment: U12 plays on a 2.60 m basket with a size 5 ball; FIBA guidance lists lower baskets for younger groups (e.g. 2.43 m for U10) and smaller or softer balls.

Under the 2026 FIBA rules, a deliberate foul to stop a fast break becomes a 'disruptive foul' that does not count towards disqualification. Coaches should re-teach transition-defence fouling policies.
In FIBA play an offensive rebound after the ball touches the ring resets the shot clock to 14, not 24. Teams should run a short 'second-chance' set rather than a full possession.
The Amsterdam 2022 consensus provides the CRT6 tool for coaches and parents to recognise suspected concussion, and SCAT6/Child SCAT6 for clinicians. Use these instead of older SCAT5 versions.

safetyReview.currentText: Keep the court clear of loose balls during drills.
safetyReview.section: No source opened on this point

safetyReview.currentText: Outdoor courts: check for wet patches and broken rims.
safetyReview.section: No source opened on this point

safetyReview.currentText: Ankle sprains are the most common injury: balance training and well-fitting shoes help; tape or bracing can help after a sprain.
safetyReview.correctedText: Ankle sprains are among the most common basketball injuries. Balance/neuromuscular training and semi-rigid or air-cast braces have the best evidence for preventing them; high-top shoes have not been shown to protect.

safetyReview.currentText: Practise soft landings with knees tracking over toes.
Stop and get assessed after any head impact.
